58_marg4: In the beginning was the Word. The substantial word is understood, which remains within in the man himself, which is understood from the sound, not the sound itself, which passes. Turn your mind to that word which you have in your heart, as a counsel born in your mind, so that your mind brings forth the counsel, and the counsel is as it were the offspring of your mind, as it were the son of your heart. For first the heart begets the counsel, that you may set up some building. The counsel is already born, and the work is not yet completed. You see what you are going to do, but another does not marvel until you have finished that work. Men look at your building and marvel at the counsel of the builder. They are amazed at what they see; they love what they do not see. If, then, human counsel is praised from some building, do you wish to see what kind of counsel God’s is? The Lord Christ, that is, the Word of God? Consider the counsel, the building of the world; see what things were made by the Word, and then you will know what kind of Word it is. Nor was the building of the world alone made by the Word, but also invisible things; and though mutable things were made by the Word, yet the Word itself is immutable. Whence he says: “In the beginning was the Word”: the selfsame, always in the same way.
58_marg5: And the Word was. Others, that he appeared suddenly among men; John says that he was always with God. Others assert a true man; John asserts a true God, saying: “And the Word was God.” Others, a man living among men in time; John says that he abides with God: “The same was in the beginning with God.” Others tell the miracles that he did as man in the world; John testifies that all things were made by him: “All things were made by him.” Behold the author of good things. “Without him was made nothing”: he is not the author of evil things.
58_marg6: In the beginning was the Word, etc. Against those who, because of Christ’s birth in time, said that Christ had not always been, he begins with the eternity of the Word, saying: “In the beginning was the Word.” ‘Word’ is said either of what is uttered and passes, as when ‘God’ or something of the kind is said, or of the thought or conception of the mind, which, born of the mind, remains with the mind itself, as when you think of the divine substance or of some other thing. By this likeness the reason and wisdom of God, which, born of God, comprehends all things, is called ‘Word’. This is said to be in the beginning, against those who say that he had not always been, because he is said to be born of the virgin in time. In the beginning, that is, in the Father, who is the beginning not from a beginning; he himself with him is the beginning from the beginning. In this only the eternity of the Word is marked, by which it goes before all things. But because others said that the same God is at one time Father, at another Son, that he may be marked as another in person he adds: “And the Word was with God,” as one with another. But because others would grant that he had always been another, but not that he was God, he adds: “And the Word was God.” But because again others would grant that he was God too, but a God made, as gods are made from men, against them he adds: “The same,” that is, the Word, “was with God.” “In the beginning,” that is, born of God before all things; in which he is shown to be co-omnipotent and consubstantial and coeternal. And after he has spoken of the nature of the Son, he adds of his working: “All things were made by him.” All things, that is, whatever is, whether in substance or in some natural property. Behold the author of good things. “And without him was made nothing,” because what is not by nature is not from him, but what is a perversion of nature, as evil or an idol. Behold, he is not the author of evil things. But lest, because these things were made mutable, the very will and reason and wisdom of God should seem to be mutable, he adds: “That which was made,” in time, and is mutable, “was” living and abiding “in him”; as a chest made in the work is changed and perishes, while the chest in the mind of the craftsman abides, so that from it one and another can be made when the one made before perishes. And so it is clear that the creature is not coeternal with the creator, but the art and reason and wisdom from which it is made is coeternal with God. Having said what the nature of the Word is and also what its working is, he adds what it does for the rational human creature. “And this life,” that is, the wisdom of God, in which all things live, “was the light,” as far as in it lies, even if the wicked do not perceive it. “Light,” that is, the enlightening of men, not of sinners or of other things. And this light indeed shines, as far as in it lies, in the dark, as the sun over a blind man; and yet those wicked men, like the blind, do not perceive the sun. For if they comprehended, they would not be darkness. But that the darkness itself might be able to comprehend, a man was promised for a witness of this light; and the light itself, that is, the Word, “was made flesh,” as it were changed into milk for the little ones. For in the form of the godhead he could not be known by the little ones.

58_marg8: Sum: the substantive verb has a twofold signification. For sometimes it declares temporal motions, after the analogy of other verbs; sometimes it designates the substance of each thing of which it is predicated, without any temporal motion. Therefore it is also called substantive. Such is what is said: “In the beginning was the Word,” as if to say, the Son subsists in the Father. For ‘was’ is put not for time but for substance.

He knew indeed that he was the Lord, that he was the Lamb taking away sins, that he himself ought to be baptized by him, as he had also confessed; but he did not know that he would keep for himself, and hand to no one, the power of baptism; and the ministry, through which the unity of the Church stands, lest there be as many baptisms as baptizers. The Lord could, however, have handed the power of baptism to some servant in his stead, so that there would be as much force in the servant’s baptism as in the Lord’s; but he willed that the hope of the baptized should be in the Lord alone, not in man, and that they should be united in him, so that there might be one dove, and it might not be divided by men. Whence the baptism of the Lord differs in nothing, whether it be given by a good or by a bad minister, nor is it repeated, because it is always the baptism of the Lord. The baptism of John is repeated, because it is not the Lord’s but man’s, even if from God. The baptism of Judas is not Judas’s but the Lord’s, and it is not repeated. And so that unity and the peace of brotherhood might be kept without rending in all the baptized, as in one dove, which moans in the hardships of the world, and carries to the ark the branch that is outside, if it has fruit: therefore the Spirit in whom one is baptized is shown through a dove. And so that, having unity and peace, they might burn within themselves against evils, he was afterwards given to the apostles in fire and in divers tongues, according to the diversity of the nations, which are now united, which were once divided from one among the proud builders. Note that in the sacrament of baptism, as in the others, Christ alone works, while the others are ministers; whence the Apostle: ‘In labour and mind they are different, in the worker not different.’
58_marg66: He shows that John did not know, through the baptism of Christ, that is, that the world was redeemed. For he knew that he was the Son of God and born in the flesh. Augustine, however, says that John did not know this: whether he would keep the power of baptizing for himself or give it to some one of his own.
58_marg67: And remaining upon him. Augustine. The Spirit is said in a special way to remain in Christ, from whom he never withdrew through sin; in whom he always lived wonderfully and worked wonderfully. He comes into the saints and withdraws through sins. Yet he always remains in them for something, as Christ promised them, namely that they may always persevere in good things. For something he does not remain, namely that by him they may prophesy or work miracles; and therefore what he says is the first sign for recognizing Christ.
58_marg68: That baptizeth. Christ baptizes in the spirit not only by remitting sins in the water, but also afterwards by cleansing, kindling love, and filling with gifts.
58_interl185: in whom there is remission, which John is not
58_interl187: the only one; whence he can baptize
58_marg69: This is the Son. He testifies that he whom he called a man above is the Son of God, so that from him there may be testimony to both natures.
58_interl188: immovable on the summit of perfection
58_marg70: The next day. Typically. John stands: the law ceases, yet bearing testimony to Christ. Jesus walks, that is, grace, gathering from this side and from that.
58_interl191: coming to us in the flesh
58_interl193: as if to say: why do you follow me? Follow him who is the Lamb of God, the price of the world
58_interl195: following the gospel, they let go of the law, using its testimony
58_marg71: They followed Jesus. They followed so as now to hear him rather than John, yet not yet cleaving to him wholly, but to see where he dwells, so that they might come to him constantly and be taught by him; and afterwards they followed perfectly, when he called them from the ship. Two follow, because those who follow ought to be kindled with a twofold charity.
58_marg72: Turning. They had seen him as it were from behind; but he showed them, as it were, his face, when he came down from his majesty so that he could be seen, when in place of the shadow of the law he displayed the light of the gospel.
58_interl197: he gives them confidence to ask
58_marg73: What seek you? He asks, not being ignorant, but that they may have a reward in answering. What? A thing, not a person; what? not whom, lest he seem to show himself; they answer with a person.
58_interl200: by this name they show their faith; they now follow him as a master
58_interl202: they do not wish to make use of him in passing, but to know the place to which they may come often and be instructed in private
58_marg74: Mystically. They wish to be shown those in whom Christ dwells, that they may make themselves like them; or, those who see the incarnation devoutly seek to be shown the eternal abode, how it is with the Father.
58_marg75: Come. As if to say: it cannot be unfolded in speech, but is shown by deed. Come by believing and by working, and you will understand; come by the testimony of John, and withdraw from the law, and you will receive grace.
58_interl203: there is no night where Christ the light is; and once one has come to him, there one must remain
58_marg76: That day. It shows the New Testament, or the present life.
58_marg77: Now it was the hour. Because they had come from the law (the decalogue sent them to Christ), at the tenth hour they seek to be taught by him, because no other teaches the law but he who gave it. And he teaches with mercy, and those things are fulfilled which could not be fulfilled. Or the tenth hour indicates the evening of the world.
58_marg78: The brother of Simon. The brother younger in birth believes first. For the order of faith is not in years. Perhaps for dignity Andrew is said to be the brother of Peter, upon whom, that is, upon whose faith, the Church was to be founded.
58_marg79: He findeth. True piety at once announces the treasure it has found to the brother, that as he is his brother in blood, he may be his brother in faith also.
58_interl206: by this word he hints that they had long sought him
58_marg80: We have found the Messias, etc. Christ in Greek, Messias in Hebrew, anointed in Latin. For he was truly anointed in a special way by the Holy Ghost, from which anointing Christians are named. For Jacob, after the vision, set up a stone for a title, which the pouring of oil anointed. Even then, by divine inspiration, through that stone he understood figuratively the rock to come, that is, Christ, who was to be anointed with the Holy Ghost; and on that rock, so anointed, he prefigured that the Church would be founded, etc.
58_interl209: the elder does not disdain to follow the younger
58_interl210: the secret of his heart; having known it, he changes his name
58_marg81: Thou art Simon the son. He first says the name he has from his parents, that the change may be signified, when he makes Peter out of Simon. In the change is marked the liveliness of the mystery; but neither is the former name without force. For Simon is ‘obedient’, ‘son of grace’ or ‘of the dove’, when he comes to Jesus following his brother. Hence from the rock, Christ, he is called Peter, firm in him, in the figure of the Church, which is founded on the rock.
58_interl212: that is, of the dove, namely the Holy Ghost, from whom he is humble, while the elder follows the younger
58_marg82: The son of Joanna, etc. He is called ‘Jona’ and ‘Joanna’ indifferently. Jona is interpreted ‘dove’, Joanna ‘grace’.
58_interl213: he does not yet bestow the name but foreshows it
58_interl214: that is, after the resurrection, to the Gentiles
58_interl215: from Judea, where John was baptizing
58_marg83: Into Galilee, etc. Galilee means ‘passing over’ or ‘revelation’. For man passes over from vices to virtues, and afterwards from virtue to virtue. And so revelation is made to him, that there may be seen “the God of gods in Sion.” Being about to call a disciple to follow, that is, to imitate, he goes out into Galilee, hinting by the place itself that as he himself advanced in wisdom, and as through sufferings he entered into glory, so too should his followers.
58_marg84: Of Bethsaida, the city. Not in vain is the city named; nor in vain is it called the city of Philip, Peter and Andrew. For it means ‘house of hunters’, in which the mind and office of these men is marked. For they are hunters in catching souls. Hence Philip, before he becomes an apostle, of his own accord calls Nathanael.
58_marg85: Philip findeth, etc. Nathanael, most skilled in the Scriptures, understands that the singular Nazarene was to come forth not from elsewhere but from Nazareth. But because he was most learned, he was not chosen as an apostle; for all the apostles were at first from the unlearned: ‘That the wise may be confounded’
58_marg86: Whom Moses wrote of. Like a wary hunter he establishes the truth to his brother by many reasons, namely that Jesus is he who is foretold in the law and the prophets; the son of Joseph, who is of the house of David, so that through him (not because he was born of him), together with Mary his mother, whom he knew from the prophets to have given birth as a virgin, he may be marked as being of David.
58_interl219: and this name is from the prophets; as also Mary, who, not unaware that she was a virgin, says: ‘I and thy father’
58_interl220: that is, of the seed of David
58_interl221: he names his native place, to mark him who, according to the prophet, shall be called ‘a Nazarene’
58_marg87: And Nathanael said to him, etc. Either he asks in doubt, or he affirms, as one skilled in the law, that from a city of so great a name there could be someone good, either an excellent teacher or the supreme Saviour.
58_marg88: For Nazareth means ‘flower’, or ‘bud of cleanness’, or ‘holiness’; and to either way of pronouncing it there is fittingly added: Come and see, etc.
58_marg89: Behold an Israelite indeed. Guile, that is, pretence. For if he has sins, he confesses them. So he does not deny that he is a sinner, but praises the confession in him. But the Pharisees are full of guile, who proclaim themselves good when they are wicked.
58_marg90: Whence knowest thou me? Knowing that the Lord speaks of his conscience, he asks not out of indignation but in wonder, whence, and by what power.
58_interl223: that is, under the tree of the fig
58_interl224: that is, under the letter of the law
58_marg91: Mystically. Nathanael, that is, gift of God, is the true people of Israel by the gift of God, which was hidden under the fig tree, that is, subjected under the habit of sinning and the shadow of death, as our first parents covered themselves under fig leaves; where it was first seen and sought by the Lord, before it saw and sought the Lord, and even before he called it through the apostles.
58_interl226: behold, the same utterance of Nathanael and of Peter; whence Peter too merited to be called
58_marg92: Rabbi, thou art, etc. Because Nathanael recognized that Christ, though absent, had seen what he himself had done in another place, that is, how and where he was called by Philip, which is a sign of deity, he confesses him not only master but also Son of God and King of Israel, that is, Christ; in which he is proved to be an Israelite, as is said, that is, one seeing God.
58_interl228: as if to say: under the fig tree you have come to faith
58_interl229: because through this small thing you have come to faith, you will come to greater things
58_marg93: You shall see the heaven. Nathanael the Israelite is said to be going to see the heaven opened and angels ascending and descending, as once the patriarch Jacob, who through the blessing was called Israel, saw a ladder and angels ascending and descending.
58_marg94: What was said to Nathanael is now fulfilled in Christians: for after the God-man ascended, the entrance of heaven is opened to those who believe in him. And they see the angels, that is, the preachers, ascending upon him when they consider and preach the secrets of the Godhead, and descending when they adapt themselves to the lowliest and preach human things of him. And it is a greater thing for them that heaven be opened and that they know both natures in him through the angels than that they were seen, that is, foreknown, while they were under the shadow of death. For if they remained there, what would it have profited them to be seen there?
58_marg95: Angels descending. This miracle often appeared, that angels ascended and descended upon Christ.
58_marg96: Upon the Son of man. Christ calls himself the Son of man, affirming what is less, namely the humanity; Nathanael and Peter call him the Son of God, which is greater, affirming the divinity. Behold the confirmation of both natures in Christ. These, confessing the Godhead, merit to ascend; he, asserting the humanity, testifies that he has come to redeem.
58_marg97: Upon the Son, etc. He confirms that he is man, lest some should err, believing him to be God only, as even Peter did when he said: “Be it far from thee, Lord.”
58_marg98: And the third day. Augustine. After Christ had been shown by the testimonies of John, he shows himself by a miracle.
58_marg99: And the third day. It signifies that on the third day, that is, in the time of grace, after the times, that is, before the law and under the law, Christ came through the flesh to the marriage of the Church.
58_interl231: The mother is a figure of the Synagogue
58_marg100: And Jesus was invited. In this he shows that marriage, which he made, is not to be despised, and he intimates the sacrament of marriage.
58_marg101: The wine failing. The wine fails so that, when wine has been wondrously made from water, the power of the hidden Godhead may appear.
58_marg102: There is greater power in the creation and governance of heaven and earth, and in this, that daily the water of the rain is turned into wine through the vines, and that crops are created from a small seed. But because these things happen naturally, they have already grown cheap from familiarity; and therefore God has reserved to himself certain things, though lesser, beyond the usual course of nature, through which the power that works also in the greater things is brought back to memory.
58_interl232: Augustine. What is there in common between my Godhead and thee, my mother according to the flesh?
58_interl233: It is the name of the sex
58_marg103: Woman, what is that to me and to thee? Augustine. In these words he does not deny his mother, as the heretics say, nor does he, who commanded us to honour parents, dishonour her; but, when she demands it, being about to work a miracle, he does not acknowledge her, as if to say: I do not work this from what thou didst bear; but I will acknowledge thee when, hanging on the cross, I as a son commit the care of thee to the disciple. But my hour is not yet come, that is, the fitting time; because the passion must not be until the gospel has been preached, until the power of the Godhead has been shown to the world; then will be the hour, not of necessity, as the heretics slander, but of will. Whence: “I have power to lay down my life, and to take it up again.” For the author of times is not ruled by the fate of time.
58_marg104: Cana of Galilee, that is, ‘zeal of passing over: there the marriage’, because those are worthy of Christ who by the fervour of devotion pass over from vices to virtues, from earth to the heavens. The mother is there, whose womb was the bridechamber from which the bridegroom came forth. And Jesus was invited by the desire of the fathers who went before, and the disciples as ministers. At the marriage ‘the wine failed’, because the sense of the law, through the carnal exposition of the Pharisees, had begun to fall away from its ancient power; but Christ turns the water into wine when he shows to be spiritual the things that seemed carnal, and made the surface of the letter be seen full of heavenly power. For Christ, not yet manifested in the prophets, lay hidden like wine in water; but when “he opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,” he made them drunk with wine and estranged their minds from the flesh. The Scriptures are the law and the prophets and the Psalms: all these according to the letter are tasteless water, according to the spirit they are wine. The six waterpots are six ages, none of which lacked prophecy. For it began from the beginning of the world. And the first age is from Adam to Noe, the second to Abraham, the third to David, the fourth to the transmigration of Babylon, the fifth to John the Baptist, the sixth to the end of the world. In these ages, then, were the waterpots, that is, the hearts of men, prepared to receive the Scriptures of God, set forth as an example of living and believing. ‘Of stone’, that is, strong in Christ the stone. According to the purifying of the Jews, that is, because the law was given to that people of the Jews, but grace through Christ was made for all. Let us see what water there was in each of the ages, as in waterpots, and how it is changed into wine. In the first, Abel is slain by his brother, and the one receives punishment, the other praise. In this, if anyone follows the innocence of Abel and flees the malice of Cain, he drinks water that washes and refreshes. But if in the same he understands Christ slain by the Jews, he drinks wine from water; and so in all the others of this age. In the second, Noe is saved in the ark for his justice; the world perishes in the flood. If anyone by this example corrects himself of vices, he drinks saving water; but if in the ark he understands the Church, which receives all the animals, that is, all nations, into the water of baptism, and other things of this kind, he drinks wine. In the third, Abraham, obedient, offers a ram in place of his son; he who learns obedience here drinks water from the third waterpot. If anyone understands in Isaac the Godhead, in the ram the flesh of Christ, he drinks wine. In the fourth, David the humble reigns, Saul the proud is cast off; in this, if anyone learns to be humbled, he drinks water. If he understands the kingdom of Christ, he drinks wine. In the fifth, the people, sinning, is taken captive and afterwards brought back; hence, if anyone learns to be corrected by penance, he drinks water. If anyone understands that the people of God is freed from the captivity of sin through Jesus, he drinks wine. In the sixth, Christ is circumcised, is offered. In this, if anyone learns to be subject to his sacraments as Christ was, he drinks water. If in the true octave he understands the laying aside of all mortality and the entrance to God, he drinks wine.
58_interl234: that is, the fitting time for showing the nature which I have from thee; but once the divine nature has been shown through miracles, the human nature too will be shown through the passion
58_interl235: although the son seems to refuse, the mother knows his kindness, and therefore confidently commands the waiters
58_interl237: metron in Greek is called ‘measure’ in Latin
58_marg105: Two or three. Augustine. To say this is the mark of one estimating, so that he should call the same ones two which he also calls three. There are therefore two measures in the Scriptures when the Father and the Son are named, and the Spirit, who is necessarily common to the Father and the Son, is understood, as: “Thou hast made all things in wisdom, O Lord,” that is, in the Son; and: “I and the Father are one.” Three, when, the Spirit being named, the Trinity is more plainly understood, as: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established; and all the power of them by the spirit of his mouth,” and: “Baptizing in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. Amen.” Otherwise, the two or three measures are all the nations to which the Scriptures belong: two because of the uncircumcision and the circumcision; the same are also three, spread abroad from the three sons of Noe.
58_interl238: because no time was empty of saving doctrine
58_marg106: And they filled them. That the waterpots were filled at his command signifies that that Scripture too is from the Lord; but, while Christ lies hidden in it under the veil, that is, under the covering of the letter, it tastes of tasteless water. But when the veil is taken away, it is inebriating wine. He who creates all things out of nothing could indeed have filled the empty ones with wine, but he preferred to make wine from water, to teach that he came ‘not to destroy the law but to fulfil it’, and that in the gospel he does or teaches nothing other than what prophecy foretold.
58_interl239: chief of the triclinium; for it is the middle space of the house, away from the walls, where the banqueters sat
58_marg107: But when he had tasted. The triclinium, that is, three ranks of those reclining at table, differing from one another in height, that is, the teachers, the continent, the married. The chief steward is some man learned in the law, who drinks the spiritual sense of the law. Whence to open the spiritual sense in the Scriptures to the disciples is to turn water into wine, as when, after the resurrection, “He opened to them their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures.”
58_marg108: The water made wine. Jerome. By the water, the baptism of John; by the wine, the passion of Christ. Whence the wine also is brought first to the chief steward, that is, to John, who drank of the passion before Christ did.
58_interl240: as Paul at first did not know the spirit in the letter
58_interl242: the carnal man goes down from true things to false
58_interl243: worldly prudence first teaches men pleasant things, then adds useless and dishonourable ones
58_interl244: because it was good formerly too, though in figures, hidden as it were in water; but now it is manifest in the gospel
58_marg109: This beginning, etc. Jerome. At the beginning of the signs which he, mortal, was to give to mortals, he turned water into wine; just as, when now immortal, he opened the understanding of the disciples, that in the law and the prophets they might understand Christ, so he first imbued carnal minds with the savour of wisdom, intending afterwards to fill them, raised again, with greater glory.
58_interl246: most beautiful town, or field of consolation
58_marg110: After this, etc. After the beginning of signs concerning the wine he adds another token of divine majesty in the casting of the sellers out of the temple. Typically. The Son of God, as humble, went down to Capharnaum, that is, into the world, according as he has a mother and brethren.
58_marg111: And the pasch was at hand, etc. We keep the pasch when we pass over from vices to virtues. To this Jesus comes when he daily visits the Church and considers the acts of each, and casts out those who, among the saints, do either good things feignedly or evil things openly. By the oxen that plough are signified the preachers of heavenly doctrine; those sell them who preach not for the love of God but for temporal gain. Sheep, innocent, give their fleeces for clothing; by these are signified the works of purity and piety, which are sold when they are done for human praise. The Spirit appeared as a dove; whence by the dove is understood the Spirit, which the simoniacs sell. They lend money in the Church who serve not heavenly things in pretence but earthly things openly. All these are cast out of the portion of the lot of the saints, who do either good things feignedly or evil things openly; and they are now scourged with the cords of sins for correction, who, if they remain uncorrected, will be bound at the end. He casts out the sheep also and the oxen, because he shows the life and doctrine of such men to be reprobate. And he overturns the tables, because at the end the very things they loved are destroyed.
58_interl249: he teaches us to keep the institutions of that Church to which we come, if it be not against the faith
58_marg112: And he went up, etc. If he who gave the decrees of God keeps them, he teaches how great a care men ought to have to give themselves to prayers and to the solemnities of God. He is read to have gone up to the pasch twice: once in the first year of his preaching, John not yet imprisoned, which is treated here; the second time when he was going to his passion; and on both occasions he cast the sellers out of the temple.
58_interl250: that they might be offered in sacrifices; and it was the avarice of the priests
58_marg113: And he found in the temple. If in the figurative temple, which is the house of prayer, he forbids trade which is thought honest, since it is in the things that are offered in the temple, how much more does he forbid drinking bouts and other graver things?
58_interl251: that the buyers might not lack the price
58_interl252: he who adds sins to sins ties, as it were, a rope with which he may be scourged and bound
58_marg114: Of little cords. The little cords with which they are cast out are the increments of evil deeds. Whence Isaias: “Woe to you that draw iniquity with cords of vanity.” And Solomon: ‘Every one is bound fast with the cords of his own sins.’
58_interl254: that is, all the matter of selling
58_interl255: the simoniac heresy is especially condemned
58_marg115: That sold doves. Not only those selling doves but others also make the house of God a house of traffic, that is: ‘All who seek the things that are their own, not the things that are Jesus Christ’s.’
58_interl256: he forbids the grace of the Spirit to be sold, because it is grace
58_interl257: here he openly calls himself the Son of God
58_interl259: because by zeal for the house of God he cast out the wicked
58_marg116: The zeal of thy house, etc. Good zeal is a fervour of soul by which the mind, human fear cast aside, is kindled for the defence of truth. He is eaten up by it who strives to correct whatever wrong things he sees; if he cannot, he bears them and groans.
58_interl260: not daring to resist him, because they saw something divine shining in his face
58_marg117: What sign dost thou shew. Because they ask a sign why the customary commerce is cast out of the temple, he says: Destroy; as if: because this temple signifies the temple of the body, in which there is no stain, I rightly cleanse this figurative one, I who am able by divine power to raise up that one when it has been destroyed by men through death.
58_interl261: he does not command, but as if he were saying: you will destroy
58_marg118: Destroy this temple. What Jesus says of his own body, which is the temple of God, I will raise it up, etc., the Jews did not understand; though ignorant, they answer by divine prompting, saying: Six and forty years was it in building, etc. For raising up befits not a stone but a man. For in forty-six days the body of Christ, as of any man, is formed in the mother’s womb; but, destroyed by the Jews, it is raised from death on the third day. This saying, behold, not even the apostles understood, until, raised on the third day, he opened it to them. But what they could not understand they bore patiently, until, by the revelation of the Holy Ghost, they saw that he had risen. Whence we take an example: that what we understand we should not lose through pride, and what we cannot understand at once we should not despise, holding it cheap, but should humbly wait, praying and exercising our minds, until we understand. For this is the way of the words of God and of the prophets: that things in them which seem open to us lie hidden, closed, lest, understood quickly, they should breed boasting, and so that, acquired by exercise, they may delight by correcting. For they are closed to the carnal sense, but given to him who labours spiritually and attends diligently, so that ‘pearls may not be cast before swine, lest they be trampled.’
58_interl262: namely, in the power of the Trinity
58_interl263: I, as God with the Father
58_marg119: Then said. Carnal men understood carnally; he was speaking spiritually, which the evangelist opens to us: But he spoke of the temple of his body.
58_marg120: Six and forty, etc. In Greek anatole is the east; dysis, the west; arctos, the north; mesembria, the south. The first letters of these four names, that is, alpha, delta, again alpha, mu, are contained in the name of Adam, who is the whole world; and alpha signifies one, delta four, again alpha one, mu forty; and together they make forty-six.
58_marg121: Built. Augustine. The building of Solomon was completed in seven years; the rebuilding under Zorobabel, with enemies hindering, in forty-six years. This number agrees with the perfection of the Lord’s body, because, as the physicians say, the form of the human body is perfected in so many days. This number is found in the letters of Adam, whose name consists of the first four letters of the regions of the world, which letters signify Adam scattered through the four parts of the world in his sons. In this number the body of Christ, which is from Adam, of which it is said, Destroy this temple, as it is also said to Adam, “Earth thou art, and into earth thou shalt go,” is built in the mother’s womb, to signify that that Adam who had been scattered was to be gathered from those four parts into one body of Christ, which is the Church. Whence it is said that the elect are to be gathered “from the four winds.”
58_interl265: that his body was to be destroyed by death and raised by himself
58_interl266: of the prophets, who said that Christ would rise on the third day
58_marg122: When he was at Jerusalem. He went to the gatherings that he might convert more by words and signs. And because some, moved by signs alone, believed in him, truly indeed, but yet so that they could afterwards be scandalized in his passion, and because they were not yet “born again of water and the Spirit,” they were not worthy that Jesus should trust himself to them and dwell with them familiarly. For he knew what was in them better than the man himself knew of himself. This faith befits the catechumens, who believe in him; but because they are not born again, the communion of the body and blood of Christ is not entrusted to them. Of such was Nicodemus, who, believing, says that he came from God because of the signs he had seen, but he was not yet born again. And therefore he came by night, not by day, because he was not yet enlightened with heavenly light.
58_interl270: not that they would do anything to him against his will, he who has “power to lay down his life,” etc., but because he knew the hidden things in them, and knew that they did not believe firmly
58_interl273: he knew in such a way as to receive nothing from anyone, since he knew of man what man himself does not know of himself
58_marg123: And there was a man. This was one of those who had believed through the signs.
58_interl274: who believe in the resurrection, by this divided from the others
58_interl275: as it were, mark the name
58_marg124: Nicodemus by name. Nicodemus means ‘victory of the people,’ or ‘victor of the people,’ bearing the figure of all who, from the Jewish people, believing in Christ, overcome the world through faith.
58_marg125: Nicodemus is either a figure of the catechumens, who have faith but are not yet baptized, who come in a kind of night of the sacraments; or he is the pattern of those who believe perfectly but yet do not yet have the light of perfect works, fearing the assault of carnal thoughts or actions, or of the unbelieving Jews, enjoying converse with Christ by faith alone, not having the confidence of good works.
58_interl278: he himself is in darkness, not light, because he is not born again
58_marg126: This man came, etc. Night signifies ‘the letter of the law,’ or ‘ignorance of heart,’ or ‘fear.’ And perhaps he came by night for this reason, that, being a master in Israel, he would have blushed to learn openly; or for fear of the Jews. This man, because he prudently noted the open signs, seeks the mysteries of faith more fully, and therefore he deserved to be taught about the godhead of Christ and his two nativities, about the passion, the resurrection and the ascension, about the second generation and the entry into the kingdom of heaven; and about many other things Jesus answered.
58_interl279: that he had come from God to the heavenly mastership, that God was with him; but that he himself was God he did not know
58_interl280: which he saw done by him at the pasch
58_marg127: Amen, amen I say to thee. To one who does not ask, he expounds the second nativity, lest Nicodemus believe that faith alone, by which he had believed in Jesus because of the signs he had seen, suffices for salvation, without the power of spiritual regeneration and without the sacraments. Also because Nicodemus understood him to be a mere man, like John the Baptist or any of the prophets, therefore Jesus began to instruct him about the second regeneration, by which he understands him to be the Son of God, and that he himself can become a son of God.
58_marg128: The second nativity of which Jesus teaches is spiritual, which is from God and the Church unto life; but he has a sense only of the carnal, which is from Adam and Eve unto death. But as he says the carnal cannot be repeated, so the spiritual too, by whomever it is done, cannot be repeated. For they are born of the seed of the true Abraham, whether through the free woman or through the bondwoman.
58_interl281: that is, unless he receive the spiritual understanding of the symbol
58_marg129: Unless a man. The visible sacrament, water, is necessary for the washing of the visible body; so the teaching of the invisible faith is necessary for the invisible sanctification of the soul.
58_interl282: which from the Greek is: from above
58_interl283: that is, he cannot know me, who am the kingdom of the Father, who am the vision of the truth
58_interl284: who knew only the carnal nativity, which cannot happen again; therefore he asks the manner of the second
58_interl285: or again, or a second time
58_interl286: he shows the manner of the second nativity
58_marg130: Of water and the Spirit. “Of water, the visible sacrament, and of the Spirit, the invisible understanding, so that he may receive the symbol of baptism visibly and fulfil the spiritual understanding of the symbol itself. Or of visible water and of the Holy Ghost.”
58_interl287: to enter is the same as to see. For he who sees enters, and he who enters sees
58_marg131: That which is born. He distinguishes this spiritual nativity from the carnal, saying: That which is born, etc.
58_marg132: Of the flesh, that is, what is from the first man by succession of the flesh is carnal. By the name of flesh he signifies not only the flesh but the whole carnal man. So, on the contrary, the whole spiritual man, soul and body, is called ‘spirit.’
58_interl288: that is, is carnal, having the nature of him who begets; it is visible and advances by invisible increments through time
58_marg133: And that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. In the word and the sacrament the Spirit is invisibly present. By this, he who was born of Adam unto death is born a son of God unto life, who is called not only spiritual but spirit, because as the substance of spirit is invisible, so invisibly, through the visible sacrament, he is made a son of God.
58_marg134: Is spirit. But do not wonder if I say that one so born is spirit, because the Holy Ghost breatheth where he will, and thou knowest not whence he cometh, and whither he goeth. So is every one that is born of the Spirit.
58_interl293: he works in whom he will, and when
58_marg135: The Spirit where. Because he has it in his power whose heart he will enlighten. Thou hearest his voice in the Scriptures, or when someone full of the Holy Ghost speaks; and even if thou hearest it, thou knowest not whence he cometh, that is, how he entered that man’s heart or how he went back, because his nature is invisible. So is every one that is born of the Holy Ghost, because, the Spirit working invisibly, he begins to be what he was not, so that the unbeliever knows not whence he cometh and whither he goeth, that is, by what grace he comes into the adoption of a son and goes into the kingdom of God. Because these things are unknown to the carnal man, he asks again: How can these things be done? Not having spiritual understanding in the letter of the law, he thinks impossible what is said of the nativity through the Spirit. Whence he is rebuked by the Lord: Art thou a master, etc.
58_marg136: And thou hearest his voice, etc. The voice of the Spirit is the voice of Christ, which Nicodemus heard; but because he is not yet born of the Spirit, he knows not whence he cometh or whither he goeth, that is, on what occasion he wills a man to be born in the Spirit, or whither he goeth, that is, to what perfection he leads the one who is born of him. For he who is born of him is made one spirit with him by grace, just as the Spirit himself is one by nature.
58_interl296: what thou sayest: thou hearest his voice, and knowest not whence he cometh, or whither he goeth
58_interl298: puffed up, thou knowest not; humble, thou shalt know
58_marg137: Art thou a master in Israel. He who is over all does not insult him so as to be held superior to him; but because he wills him to be born of the Spirit, which he cannot be unless he is humble, he humbles him, swollen as he was from his mastership. As if: Proud ruler, thou knowest nothing; humble thyself, like him who emptied himself, and, born of the Spirit, thou shalt know what now thou knowest not.
58_interl299: we: that is, I with the prophets and apostles
58_marg138: What we know we speak, that is, because he himself is the knowledge, the speech and the word of the Father; and what we have seen we testify, because he himself is the vision and the true testimony and the truth of the Father. The plural hints at the mystery of the Trinity.
58_interl302: that is, you carnal men do not believe our testimony
58_interl303: that is, if you do not believe the destruction and resurrection of the earthly body, why do you seek to have the mysteries of the spiritual birth opened?
58_marg139: If I have spoken to you earthly things. Augustine. And since you do not receive earthly things, how can you grasp heavenly things, that is, the heavenly birth of the Spirit? For you not only do not believe but do not even understand the earthly things I spoke of the temple of my body, which I took from the earth: that it would be destroyed by you and raised up by me.
58_interl304: as if: yet I will speak heavenly things
58_marg140: And no man hath ascended. After he has rebuked him and invited him to humility, because this man attends diligently to what he has heard, he instructs him further about heavenly and earthly things. His ascension to life is heavenly; his lifting up on the cross to death is earthly. As if: understand the heavenly things, which carnal men do not, and understand the same of the ascension. For those reborn spiritually will ascend into heaven, but not unless they are members cleaving to him who in one person is man and the Son of God; so that this man may know that no one can ascend of himself, but through Christ. And therefore he does not say that men ascend, but the Son of man, whole with the body, who according to the Godhead descended from heaven, and is in heaven, not according as he is man. And because this ascension cannot be except for those redeemed by the passion, he therefore adds:
58_marg141: But he that descended. This belongs to the second birth, in the Spirit, because no one ascends in Christ to the Father except him who is born of the Spirit. No one is saved by the death of Christ except him who is born of the Spirit. No one is born of the Spirit except in the death of Christ. And when he says “the Son of man,” he gives us certainty of ascending, since we are sons of men.
58_interl307: because the same is also the Son of God
58_marg142: And as Moses. He adds concerning his death, which is the origin and cause of having the things said before, and in faith in it he instructs him. And because he was carnal and known in the law, he therefore brings forward a certain part of the law, which he shows to be a figure, signifying his death, so that thus it may be plain of the other parts of the law too that they are in figure. And because death is understood by “the serpent,” and Christ dead is called “a serpent”: whoever looks on him by faith is freed, as by looking on that one in the figure they were freed from the fiery serpents, which signify the incitements of vices.
58_interl309: as if: in this way that will be done, namely by the death of Christ
58_marg143: So must be lifted up, etc. He invites the master of the law to the meaning of the law; and because he had spoken of the Son of man, lest Nicodemus think him this only, he adds that the same is also the Son of God, saying: “For God so,” etc.
58_interl311: that is, looks upon him with true faith
58_interl312: this through the Son of man, because the same is the Son of God, sent for this out of the love of God: “For God so loved,” etc.
58_marg144: For God so, etc. He opens the cause of human salvation, namely the love of God the Father, and that all restoration is through his Son in the Holy Ghost.
58_marg145: World. The Greek “cosmos,” which in Latin is “mundus,” is interpreted “adornment.” By the world, then, human nature is signified: not because according to the body it consists of the four elements, but because according to the soul it is adorned by God and made to the image of God; which God loves to this end, that he may make it eternal.
58_interl314: unto death, that every one looking upon his death may not perish but may have life everlasting
58_marg146: As to give his Son. Behold, he says the same of the Son of God as he said above of the Son of man, so that through the same one through whom we were created in the Godhead, we may be restored in the man.
58_interl315: truly salvation is through the Son of God; for he came for no other cause but to save, not to judge, that is, condemn
58_marg147: To judge, etc. Judgment has not yet appeared, but judgment has already been made. “The Lord knoweth who are his.” For judgment, that is, eternal damnation, is nothing other than not to know and not to believe in the Son of God; as blessedness and life are nothing other than to believe and know the Son of God. Whence it is said: “This is eternal life: That they may know thee, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.”
58_interl317: whence he is called “the Saviour of the world”
58_marg148: But that the world may be saved, etc. From him man is saved, not judged; but if he is judged, he has it from himself, because he did not believe.
58_interl318: because through faith the sins are forgiven for which he would be condemned
58_interl321: in whom alone is salvation; God does not have many sons through whom he might save
58_marg149: And this is the judgment. Why is he that does not believe judged? Because the light has come, which rouses men and admonishes them to know their own evils, in which all are; but some hate the light that admonishes them, and flee it, lest their evils, which they love, be reproved. Others, admonished by the light, accuse their own evils, which is to do the truth, and so they are enlightened.
58_interl324: this is the ground of damnation
58_marg150: For their works were. He who is in darkness and loves the light is not evil; but he is called “evil,” and his works evil, who after the light has come hates the light and loves evil things. And this is what he says: “For their works were evil.” Works, that is, impiety and unbelief and hatred of the eternal light, and not wishing to look upon it, but wishing to remain in the darkness of sins.
58_interl331: who is in the intention of evil, and whom evil pleases
58_interl333: He does not join himself to the light but flees it.
58_interl334: the evil things which he loves
58_interl335: that is, the good works which the truth commands
58_marg151: But he that doth. Having shown by what justice he who does not believe is condemned, he shows by what justice he who believes is saved.
58_marg152: But he that doth truth, that is, he whom his evil deeds displease and who accuses them, does not pardon himself, does not spare himself, but comes to the light. And he who accuses his evil deeds begins to act with God, because the beginning of good is the accusation of evil. Therefore his works are these, namely that he accuses himself as God accuses; this he makes manifest, because they are done in God; for unless the light of God shone on him, he would not be displeasing to himself.
58_interl336: namely the Pasch, and the things done which he has narrated here
58_marg153: After these things. Not immediately after the disputation with Nicodemus, which took place in Jerusalem; but after a space of time had passed he returned from Galilee into Judea.
58_interl337: it signifies those who confess, whom Christ visits
58_marg154: Into Judea. Morally. Where there is confession of sins or of divine praises, thither come Jesus and his disciples, that is, his teaching and enlightenment, where he abides, cleansing from offences. Whence follows: “and there he abode with them, and baptized.”
58_interl338: that is, with the disciples, or with the Jews believing in him
58_interl340: with his own baptism, not that with which he was baptized; for he underwent that so that it might be the way and preparation for his own baptism.
58_marg155: And baptized. As much as the teaching of the faith profits catechumens not yet baptized, so much did the baptism of John profit before the baptism of Christ. For as he preached penance and foretold the baptism of Christ, and also drew men to the knowledge of the truth which appeared to the world, so the ministers of the Church first instruct those coming to the faith, afterwards reprove their sins, then promise remission in the baptism of Christ, and so draw them to the love and knowledge of the truth.
58_interl341: running before and preparing for the baptism of Christ
58_marg156: And John also was. While Christ is already baptizing, John still baptizes, because the shadow still remains. Nor ought the forerunner to cease until the truth is made manifest. Mystically: the consummation of the letter of the law had not yet come.
58_marg157: In Ennon. “Ennos” in Greek, “water” in Latin. Whence, as if opening the interpretation of the name, he adds: “because there was much water there.”
58_marg158: Near Salim. Salim is a town situated beyond the Jordan, where Melchisedech once reigned.
58_interl343: Mystically. The consummation of the letter of the law had not yet come, but when, hanging on the cross, he said: “It is consummated.”
58_marg159: For John was not yet. Behold, he plainly notes the deeds of Christ before John was imprisoned, which the others passed over, beginning from the things done after John was cast into prison, when, the baptism of the forerunner ceasing, the baptism of Christ openly began.
58_interl344: defending their master’s baptism and thinking John greater than Christ
58_marg160: And there arose. While John preaches and his school lasts, Christ preaches and works secretly but baptizes openly, so that a question may arise about the baptism of John and the baptism of Christ, and that it may be resolved by the testimonies of John.
58_interl345: who said the baptism of Christ was better, to which John invited men, and not Jesus to John’s
58_interl346: that he might resolve this question
58_marg161: And they came to. Wishing to accuse Christ, whom a little before they had seen baptized by John.
58_interl347: as if they would stir him to envy against Jesus
58_interl352: as if: what do you think of this presumption?
58_marg162: John answered. Because I was born beyond the custom of human nature, of parents of advanced age, you think me to be beyond men. But know that I am a mere man; he is God, from whom I have whatever I have. From me is weakness, from him the sublimity of grace. Do you think that I would say anything against my own testimony? I do not baptize unto the remission of sins, but he does.

58_interl355: not, then, greater than he, but sent before, as a herald, a servant preparing the way for him

58_interl356: What then are you? What is he? I am the friend of the bridegroom, who am jealous for the bride for him, not for myself
58_interl357: that is, the Church, which brings forth and remains a virgin
58_interl359: the humble does not fall, but the proud
58_interl361: not of himself, in whom there is sadness, but of God
58_interl362: that is, his testimony, by which he declares himself the Son of God, the bridegroom of the Church
58_interl363: so therefore I too rejoice at the voice of the bridegroom, because he himself enlightens me

58_interl364: that is, I have my grace; my grace suffices me; I take no more to myself, lest I lose what I have received
58_interl365: and do not wonder that he baptizes more than I, because
58_marg166: He must increase. I rejoice at the voice of the bridegroom. He, the bridegroom, will increase, that is, he will be found to be the Christ, who was thought a prophet. I shall decrease, because I shall be found to be his prophet, who was thought the Christ.
58_marg167: He must increase. That is, be exalted, that is, while he forgives sins and gives grace; in which his glory, which in itself is always perfect, increases in man while man sees and has it more. Man is decreased, who before gloried in himself, when now he confesses his sins and receives what he gives. The passion of each bears witness to this thing: Christ is exalted on the cross; John is diminished by the head. Creation also bears witness: John was born when the days were decreasing, but Christ when they were increasing.
58_marg168: But I. John is the figure of the law, Christ the truth; the law is diminished when the truth appears.
58_marg169: [1] He that cometh from above, that is, from the height of human nature before the sin of the first parent; for from that height the Word of God assumed human nature, and did not assume the guilt whose penalty he assumed. [2] For he who comes from heaven, that is, from the Father, is above all in two ways: first, above all humanity, since he came from it as it was before it sinned; second, according to the height of the Father, to whom he is equal.
58_marg170: Of the earth. That is, he who is born of earthly parents, from whom he contracted sin and the penalty of sin, of himself is nothing but earth.
58_interl374: and behold, he savours and speaks earthly things; but if divine things, it is from him who enlightens him
58_interl375: this is what he said before: “from above”
58_marg171: And what he hath seen. Since the Son of God himself is the Word of the Father, he does not hear another Word of the Father or testify it to men, but himself, the Word which the Father spoke, that is, brought forth and begot from himself; he knows this and shows to men that he is from the Father. This the evangelist says as he could, which cannot be fully said or understood.
58_interl380: of the people on the left
58_interl381: of the people on the right
58_interl382: he himself who descended from heaven and is above all
58_marg172: Hath set to his seal. That is, he has placed a sign in his heart as something special, namely that this is the true God, who was sent for the salvation of men.
58_interl383: truly true, because he speaks the words of God
58_marg173: True. “Every man” of himself “is a liar,” for he cannot speak true things unless enlightened by God. For he whom God the Father hath sent speaketh the words of God. What is that? He whom God sent is God. Therefore he speaks the words of God; therefore the words of the Son, bearing testimony of himself that he is God, are the words of God.
58_marg174: Speaketh the words of God. In this he distinguishes himself from Christ; but because he was sent and speaks the words of God, he adds more openly: “For not by measure.”
58_marg175: Not by measure. To men he gives by measure; to the Son he does not give by measure, but as he begot his Son whole from his whole self, so to his incarnate Son he gave his whole Spirit, not piecemeal, not by subdivisions, but generally and universally; and he gives for no other reason than that the Father loves the Son.
58_interl388: so that the Son may be as great as the Father; for he begot him equal to himself
58_marg176: He that believeth. As if he said: He that believeth in the Son has the Son himself, and through this has life.
58_marg177: But the wrath of God. The wrath with which he was born abides; and therefore he does not say ‘comes’ but ‘abides’, because through the Son who was sent, who is life, the effect of that wrath is not taken away, namely death, corruption, etc., all of which abide.
58_marg178: When therefore. Jesus knew their knowledge and their envy: that they had learned of him not in order to follow him but to persecute him; and therefore he fled, teaching his own to yield to the wicked, not fearing them nor unable to escape them.
58_interl392: by whose counsel John was taken
58_interl393: that is, the disciples of John, who were mostly of the Pharisees
58_marg179: And baptizeth. Which is truly said. For he himself always cleanses in the Spirit, invisibly and by gift; but his baptism is also done in the body, which consists in two things, namely in water and the word of life. Whence Paul: “Cleansing it by the laver of water and the word of life.”
58_marg180: But his disciples. In whose baptism the Spirit was given, though not so manifestly as he was given after the ascension, in an ineffable and inconceivable manner.
58_interl396: it signifies the passing over from the Jews to the Gentiles
58_marg181: He left Judea. That is, the unbelieving Pharisees, who were thinking to persecute him on account of his baptism, which was growing, and because they understood that by his teaching the law was being made void.
58_marg182: And went. After he had received a few of the Jewish people, he left the unbelievers who follow the letter of the law, which leads no one to perfection. And he went into Galilee, that is, into the spiritual understanding of that letter.
58_interl397: because he had come from Galilee into Judea
58_marg183: Into Galilee. In Galilee the transfiguration of the Lord is believed to have taken place, by which is signified the changing of human nature into its former glory. In Galilee he gave the disciples teaching on the mountain, by which believers are to pass over to life.
58_interl398: he shows that as he preached to the Jews, he preached also to the Gentiles
58_marg184: He was of necessity. Between Judea and Galilee is Samaria; that is, between the law of the letter, which is meant by Judea, and the divine laws turned about God, whose figure is Galilee, the natural law is set in the middle. Since therefore he took the foundations of the Church from the law, he had to pass over to the Gentiles, who were set under the law of nature, so that with both he might return into the Galilee of eternal blessedness.
58_interl399: that is, into the gathering of the faithful from the Gentiles
58_marg185: He cometh therefore. That the Samaritans, who claimed for themselves the inheritance of the patriarch Israel, might know him and be converted to him.
58_marg186: Which is called Sichar. Sichar, that is, ‘shutting up’ or ‘branch’: that is, the Gentile people, shut up under sin, which is the branch cut from the wild olive and grafted into the olive.
58_interl401: in figure of Christ, who is the lawful heir of the patriarch, having his inheritance among the Gentiles
58_marg187: Now there was, etc. Because natural reason springs from nowhere else than from the cause of all good things, therefore it is beautifully said that Jacob’s well was there, that is, reason proceeding from the infinite height of the Father.
58_interl403: for he took on all things that belong to our infirmity, without sin
58_marg188: Allegorically. The journey of Jesus is ‘the taking on of flesh’, in which there is weariness, that is, weakness, raising up man, whom he created by his power. The sitting is ‘humility’. The sixth hour: ‘the sixth age’, in which he came. The well: the depth of this world. The Samaritan woman: ‘the Church comes, not now righteous but to be made righteous’. The water of the well: ‘the pleasure of this world’, which is drawn up as from the depth by men stooping and bending down to it, with cupidity let down before them like a waterpot.
58_interl404: the journey of Christ: the incarnation
58_marg189: Sat. As it were relieving weariness; in which is shown the master who would teach those who came to him and possess them.
58_marg190: On the well. It is called a spring wherever water flows from the earth; but if it is on the surface, it is only a spring; if in the depth, it is also called a well.
58_interl405: by which the fervent faith of the Samaritans
58_marg191: There cometh. In figure of the Church from the Gentiles, which before was drawing water, that is, pleasure, from the depth of the world; whose faith Jesus thirsts for, and he asks to be given drink by her.
58_marg192: Or the woman, that is, the Synagogue, which comes to draw water, that is, to learn the history of the letter of the law; whose faith Jesus asks for. The well is deep: ‘the depth of the mysteries of the law’; or ‘husbands’, or ‘the books of Moses’; ‘he whom thou now hast’, that is, the book of Josue. She left her waterpot, that is, her former way of life; she went into the city, that is, the primitive Church.
58_marg193: Give me to drink. Jesus, sitting upon the well, asks of the primitive Church, which he had chosen from the Gentiles, the drink of faith by which he may be believed in; he asks of nature the drink of reason by which the creator and redeemer may be searched out. The apostles were sent into the city, that is, into the world, to buy spiritual meats, that is, faith and action and knowledge, with which the masters of the Church are filled.
58_marg194: Give me to drink. Though Jesus could thirst after his weariness, yet he does not require this drink; but he desires that the heart of the Church of the Gentiles, in acknowledgment of his labour, be made drink for him.
58_marg195: For his disciples. The disciples went into the city, namely to the Jews, who were fortified by the rampart of the law and armed with the darts of prophecy, to buy their meats, namely preparing their hearts for God by the preaching of faith.
58_marg196: The woman saith to him. Not knowing what drink he asks of her, and thinking it is of water, she objects that she belongs to the foreign vessels, whose company the Jews do not even use; but Jesus, who was asking for faith, desired to give her the Spirit, and admonishes her to ask; and the Spirit is both the gift of God and living water.
58_interl406: she knew him by his dress
58_interl408: because they disagreed about the place of prayer
58_marg197: For the Jews do not communicate. The Jews curse the Samaritans and call them supplanters, because they had formerly deprived them of the inheritance of their Jacob; abstaining from their food and vessels.
58_marg198: Jesus answered. Step by step and with simple words he instructs her, so that at length she may be able to receive the gift of God, that is, the Spirit.
58_interl409: which is the Spirit of God
58_interl411: that is, asks faith of thee
58_interl412: understand: living water, that is, the Spirit, through whom faith also would be given
58_marg199: The woman saith to him. No water is called living but that which is taken up where it springs; of which the woman, wise after the flesh, said: Since thou hast nothing to draw with, and the well is deep, how hast thou living water? But lest perhaps he should seem to promise another spring, she adds: Art thou better? That is, canst thou be better than Jacob, who with his own used this one? Against this, therefore, Christ shows openly that he speaks not carnally but spiritually, saying that he who has drunk his water does not thirst.
58_interl415: which could not be had unless it were drawn from the bottom of the well
58_marg200: Art thou. Though a foreigner, she calls Jacob her father, because she had lived under the law of Moses and possessed the land which Jacob had given to his son.
58_interl418: drawing up water with a vessel
58_marg201: And drank thereof himself. From the well men and cattle drink; likewise from reason, which, as it were depraved and darkened, is dug and worked with great labour. Some drink like men, who use that reason for good, as the saints; some like cattle, who use it for evil, as the philosophers.
58_interl419: by whom are meant the more perfect in the Church
58_interl420: the lesser, or those altogether ignorant
58_interl422: namely for the pleasure of the world, which such water signifies
58_marg202: But he that shall drink. Whoever shall apply his heart to my preaching and shall know the gift of grace, in him is born “faith that worketh by charity”, and so at length he will pass into life everlasting.
58_interl423: he promises the fullness of the Spirit, which will come about in the resurrection, because with him is “the fountain of life”, with which they shall be inebriated

58_marg208: For thou hast had five husbands. The five husbands are five laws given to human nature. The first in paradise before sin, in the prohibition of the tree. The second after the transgression and the expulsion from paradise, concerning the multiplication of human offspring. The third to Noe before the flood, concerning the building of the ark. The fourth after the flood, concerning the divisions of the nations. The fifth to Abraham, concerning circumcision and the sacrifice of his son. To these, whether laws or as it were husbands, the human soul was subject from the beginning of the world until Moses. Afterwards was given the law of the letter, which conferred no salvation; whence it is said: “He whom thou now hast, is not thy husband.” Leave the letter, go to the spirit of the letter, to the New Testament, from which thou mayest conceive a spiritual offspring of virtues.
58_marg209: Five husbands, that is, or, the senses of the body, have ruled thee; now, in the time of discretion, no husband rules thee, that is, the understanding of wisdom, but an adulterer, that is, error, corrupts thee, while thou takest carnally what I say; and therefore: “Call thy husband”, so that, as I say, thou mayest understand spiritually. The five senses are called husbands in the younger age for this reason, that they are lawful. 58_marg247: Probathon is Greek; in Latin it is called sheep. Probatica, therefore, is the pool for flocks, because there the carcasses of the victims were washed. That water signifies “the people of the Jews,” who now stands quiet, now is troubled by the winds of temptations, who say to the Lord: “We are thy people, and the sheep of thy pasture.” The five porches, that is, the law which is in five books, are indicated. There are many sick there, because the law does not heal but exposes the sick, so that at some time they might seek a physician. There are blind there, who do not have the light of faith; lame, who cannot work what they see; dry, who, whatever they do, are without the fatness of charity. “Waiting for the moving of the water,” in which health was made by an angel, because joined to the law they desired the grace of redemption. The angel is the Son of God, hidden in flesh among the Jews, who were stirred by his teachings to persecute him; by whose death the unity is healed, which descends through humility to the faith of the passion. 58_marg262: And Jesus answered and said to them. Because they were moved by hearing of his equality, he whom they thought a mere man, with God the Father, he subjoins that he is the Son, equal to the Father, of the same will, the same power, the same operation. In arguing these matters he uses this kind of speech, by which he can stir up the minds of little ones, and if not fill them, at least by which the minds of adults are exercised and fed. For he speaks of the deity of the Son: “The Son cannot do any thing of himself, but what he seeth the Father doing”; and “the Father shows him all things,” which are to be taken not according to the letter, as if it were done in men, but mystically. To them, however, he says these secrets so that they may be confounded, or that, perhaps troubled, they may seek a physician. For our sake too, that those things were written for us which, not well understood, would lead into error, and, well understood, would lead into truth.

Or two fish: two persons set over the government of the people, the royal and the priestly, who are tossed about among the crowds of the surging people yet do not fail; in them one Christ is signified, king and priest. Grass, because they tasted carnally; in carnal things they rested. But to those to whom Christ the king and priest has come, they trample the flesh so as to be refreshed otherwise, in spirit. But the men, that is, the more perfect who are worthy of number apart from weak age and frail sex, are five thousand, that is, perfectly; or they have dominion over the bodily senses, and these are refreshed by Christ. He took the loaves: he did not create new ones, because he did not dissolve the ancient Scripture but fulfilled and taught it. “He gave thanks”: teaching us to give thanks for all benefits, and showing that he rejoices in our refreshment and salvation. “He multiplied,” because from those few so many Scriptures have come forth. The fragments are the more secret things, which the common people do not grasp; these the apostles gather, and they are entrusted to those cast off from the world and perfect in heart. Seeing the prophet, they call him so, perhaps because they still sit in the grass. But he is also truly called “prophet,” because when he teaches something present he is called angel, when he foretells the future, prophet. 58_marg396: It was his custom to teach in the temple by day, and in the evening to return to Bethania, which is on the Mount of Olives. Mystically he signifies the height of mercy, whence for us is the chrism, that is, the anointing. He returns to the temple in the morning. ‘Morning’ is the rising of a new light after the darkness of the law, by which he comes to pour out and give mercy to the faithful, that is, in his temple. ‘Sitting’ is the humility of the incarnation, by which he has pity and teaches, whence the people come more willingly to him. But the enemies, the Pharisees, test him about justice, whether he will speak against it. They knew him to be meek and a preacher of mercy, whence he pleased the people; so they thought he would say that the adulteress should be dismissed, and that in this case he would be called an enemy of the law, contrary to Moses and to God the author, and a man guilty of death along with the adulteress. But if he said she should be stoned according to the law, they would mock him, as though he did not have the meekness he preached, by which he was loved. But he is caught in neither accusation, and, keeping his meekness, answers what is truly just: ‘He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.’ He does not judge at once, but bending down he writes with his finger on the ground. The law was written with the finger of God on stone because of that people’s hardness; now, bent down as a man, he himself is the guardian of the law and its bearer, writing on the earth, which bears fruit. He teaches us, when we hear of someone’s faults, not to judge rashly, but first to examine ourselves inwardly with the finger of discernment, as he says to them: ‘He that is without sin among you.’ As if to say: first be just, so that afterwards you may punish the guilty woman. For if the law orders the guilty to be punished, it is not therefore to be done by those who are to be punished in like manner. Behold, full justice: that the just man punish evil. Let them therefore either dismiss the guilty woman or undergo the penalty with her.

58_marg554: Before six days. All mystically. Sixth, because he made all things in six days; on the sixth day he made man; in the sixth age he came to redeem; on the sixth day of the week he suffered; at the sixth hour he died. He came to Bethania, that is, to ‘the house of obedience’: he himself obedient to the Father unto death, teaching the Church obedience, which is on the mount of olives, that is, of mercy, and cannot be hidden, in which he raises up those buried in grave sins. There the supper is made in the faith and devotion of the just. Martha serves, that is, while every faithful person devotes works of devotion to the Lord. Lazarus, that is, those raised from grave sins, together with those who remained in justice, joyfully feast in the presence of the Lord. Mary, who once as a penitent anointed the feet, and where it is not said with what ointment: now the feet and head with precious ointment; there he designates the beginnings of penitents, here the justice of the perfect. Whence here a pound of ointment, that is, the perfection of justice. Ointment, because: “We are the good odour of Christ unto God.” She anoints the head, who preaches lofty things of him; the feet, who reveres the weak; she wipes with her hair, who refreshes with his surplus the poor who are in need on earth. 58_marg600: Pasch is equivocal among the Greeks. For it is said both from paschein, that is, from suffering, and from passing over, which the Hebrews call Phase. The fourteenth day, after the vernal equinox, on which the lamb was sacrificed in the evening, was properly called ‘Pasch from passing over.’ The following days of the festival, of which the first and last were held in greater honour, were properly called ‘days of unleavened bread.’ Yet the day of the sacrifice is also called ‘azyma,’ and the fifteenth Pasch. In this sense John says, ‘Before the festival day of the Pasch,’ calling the solemn day ‘Pasch.’ But the Greeks say that only the day on which the lamb is sacrificed is called ‘Pasch,’ and they say that on that day Christ was crucified at midday. And they say that he anticipated it by one day, so that he might eat the lamb with his disciples; and the following words support this, namely: ‘They would not enter the judgment hall, that is, Pilate’s house, lest they be defiled, but that they might eat the Pasch,’ understanding Pasch to mean the eating of the lamb. Nor are they ashamed to say that the other evangelists lied, who say that the Lord ate the flesh of the lamb with the others in the usual way. They say John corrected them. But they are wrong, because since it is agreed that all spoke by the same Spirit, if they lied in one, they would not be believed in the others.

58_marg627: Now is the Son of man glorified. Augustine. With Judas gone out, of whom it was said: “You are not all clean,” only the clean remained with their cleanser, in which the glorifying of Christ was signified, in which, the evil being separated off, he will remain for eternity with the saints. So signifying things are called by the names of the things signified, as it is not said of the rock, “it signified Christ,” but “it was Christ.” So by this act of separating Judas, bearing witness to that future separation, he says: “Now,” not “the glorifying is signified,” but: “Now is the Son of man glorified, and God is glorified in him,” because it is not he in himself but God who is glorified in him. And “God also will glorify him in himself,” so that the human nature, united to the Word, may be given immortal eternity also. For if they believe in God not as he is, but as something else, I know not what, that they suspect him to be, and hate this, surely they do not hate him, but what they conceive by their lying suspicion or false belief. If they think of him what he truly is, how are they said not to know him? And this can happen with men, or in men. For we can love or hate even those we have not seen, but not those unknown: for even if unseen, their goodness or badness is known by report or by letters; and if we love good things and hate evil things, and so do not err in judgment of things, it is venial. If we do not think true things about the hidden matters of men (which is a human temptation), and suspect them to be otherwise than they are, then, if such suspicions are human, judgment about such things, that is, a defined and certain sentence, is forbidden. From suspicions it comes about that a good man, if he thinks a good man evil, hates him, not knowing; and not knowing, he even loves an evil man. So too the evil man, to whom goodness displeases, hates the good; and if he thinks an evil man good, not knowing, he loves him.

But “whatever he shall hear, he shall speak”: he shall hear from him from whom he proceeds; to hear from him is to know, and that is to be. From whom, then, he has his essence, from him he has his hearing, that is, his knowing, which is nothing other than his essence, etc. Of an eternal thing it is properly said is; for us it is rightly said was, is, will be, was, because it never was not. Since therefore our speech varies with time, words of every tense are truly said of him, because at no time was he absent, is he absent, or will he be absent.
