58_marg857: And that night. But that night signifies the coming of Christ, in which no one comes to perfection through the law. The morning of the coming stood now after the resurrection, on the solid shore outside the waves, and it is not recognized at first. In this narrative there is a great sacrament, and it is written in the last place so that it might be more strongly commended. That the disciples in the fishing were seven signifies “the end of time,” which turns on seven days. The shore too, since it is the end of the sea, signifies “the end of the age,” in which Peter drew in the net at the beginning of Christ’s preaching. There is another catch here, another after the resurrection. There both good and bad were taken, as the Church now has them; here only the good, who will be forever, the resurrection of the dead being fulfilled at the end. There Jesus does not stand on the shore as here, but goes up into Simon’s boat. There fish in little boats; here the net on land. There, therefore, the Church in this age; here, at the end of the age. There the called; here the raised. There the nets not only on the right or on the left, lest only the good or only the bad be taken, but indifferently, so that good and bad are held mixed; here on the right, so that only the good are taken. There the net is broken by schisms; here, in the highest peace of the saints, it is not torn. There such a multitude that it sinks the boats, that is, presses them down into submersion, for they are not sunk. Here they cannot drag the net for the multitude of fish, so as to pour out the catch into the boat as there, because those who belong to the resurrection of life, after the end of this life, are in the sleep of peace, lying as it were hidden in the deep, and will not appear except when they have risen on the shore, that is, at the end of the age. What there is figured by two little boats, for circumcision and uncircumcision, is here figured by the net drawn up two hundred cubits, for the elect of both kinds, as it were a hundred and a hundred, because this number passes to the right. There the number is not stated, because they were multiplied beyond number; here there is a fixed number: one hundred and fifty-three. Ten signifies “the law,” which kills; seven, “the Spirit,” which gives life. Let the Spirit then be added to the law that it may be fulfilled, that is, the seven to the ten, and there are made seventeen; which number, counting all from one up to itself, growing, reaches one hundred and fifty-three. By it is signified all who belong to the grace of the Spirit, which grace is reconciled with the law of God as with an adversary, so that, the Spirit giving life, the letter does not kill but is fulfilled, and if anything is lacking, it is forgiven. This number has one hundred and fifty, and moreover three, because of the ministry of the Trinity. Fifty, moreover, is made by seven multiplied by seven, and by the addition of one. By the one is signified the unity of those shown through the seven, because of the sevenfold working; and on that day the Spirit was sent to the apostles. In the first catch, which is of the present Church, great and small. In that kingdom, none but the great.

58_marg870: By not naming him, John is distinguished from the others; not because he loved him alone, but because he loved him more than the others. The sign of this greater love is that he alone reclined upon Jesus’ breast. But Peter loved Christ more, as he himself, knowing it, asks, saying: “Lovest thou me more than these?” He therefore seems better who loves Christ more than he who loves him less; likewise he seems better who is loved more by Christ than he who is loved less; and John is preferred to Peter. But if, comparing them with each other, one asks which of the two is better: is it he who loves Christ less and is loved more by him, or he whom Christ loves less though he himself loves him more? The answer is doubtful. Indeed he who loves Christ more seems better; he whom Christ loves more is happier. There is evident mercy, but hidden justice, in that the one who loves less is loved more, and the one who loves more is loved less. But through these two he commends the two lives of the Church, of which he speaks mystically. One is through faith, the other through hope. This is lived in the body and in pilgrimage, where blessedness is only in hope, but misery is at hand from adversities and sins. That one is in immortality, where there is no evil but the perfection of good. The first, the active life, is signified by Peter, who is a general figure founded on the rock, Christ. To him is said: “Follow thou me,” by imitation, in enduring temporal evils, which will end with the world. This one loves Christ more, so that by loving and following he may be freed from evil; but Christ himself loves this life, as it now is, less, and frees it so that it may not always be such, and loves it for no other reason than to save it and transfer it hence. The other, the contemplative, is signified by John, to whom it is said: “So I will have him to remain.” It is not said “to remain” or “to abide” but “to wait,” because it will be fulfilled not now but when Christ has come. As if to say: let the begun contemplation remain till I come, to be perfected when I have come, so that the fullness of knowledge may be manifest. Christ fully loves this, and keeps it for eternity. In that waiting, however, since man does not yet know the future truth, he loves less, and he will love more when he sees him as he is. Moreover, since “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth,” the just man, who in this life has experienced evils on every side, loves more out of the necessity by which he is pressed than out of the mercy by which he is to be freed from evils; he asks and has daily; and he is loved less by the merciful one, who loves the wretched less than the blessed. This is Peter: loving more, and loved less. But since the just man does not yet know the contemplation of truth, which is future, he loves it less than wretched Peter loves mercy; and blessed in that very truth, he will be fully loved by Christ; and this is John: loving less than Peter, yet loved more. And if these two apostles each signify one of these two lives, nevertheless each life belongs to both of them, as also to all the saints. But to the helm of this stormy life the keys are given for binding and loosing sins. But because of that quiet rest, one reclines upon the breast of Jesus, whence truth is drunk. John, who is a virgin, belongs to the future life, where “they shall neither marry, nor be married.”
